chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Abd al-A'la said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'My father used to say: Whoever visits this House as a pilgrim or a visitor, free from arrogance, will return from his sins as he was on the day his mother gave birth to him.'
Then he recited: 'So for whoever hastens [his departure] in two days, there is no blame upon him; and for whoever delays [for another day], there is no blame upon him — for whoever fears Allah.'
I asked: What is arrogance? He said: 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: Indeed, the greatest arrogance is the dismissal of truth and the folly regarding truth.'
I asked: And what is the dismissal of truth and the folly regarding truth? He said: 'Disregarding the truth and thrusting at its people, and whoever does that competes with Allah for His cloak.'

key_terms.سَفَهُ الْحَقِّ: Folly or foolishness regarding the truth
key_terms.غَمْصُ الْحَقِّ: Dismissal or slighting of the truth
key_terms.نَازَعَ اللَّهَ رِدَاءَهُ: Competes with Allah for His cloak (a metaphor for claiming divine attributes or authority)

ai.seo_question: What is the definition of arrogance (kibr) in Shia hadith and how does it affect the acceptance of Hajj?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) narrates that his father taught that a pilgrim free from arrogance (al-kibr) returns from their Hajj or Umrah with sins erased as if reborn. Arrogance is defined as dismissing the truth and acting foolishly towards it, a state where one competes with Allah for His cloak. This tradition highlights the spiritual prerequisite of humility in ritual worship, linking the physical act of pilgrimage to the internal purification of the ego, a core theme in Shia ethical jurisprudence.
